A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ -10 & 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ -10 & 20\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-20 & -10 \\ -10 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ -10 & 20\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ -10 & 20\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

  

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$ 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-4I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$

$$

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.

$$

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \dfrac{1}{\sigma_i} A\mathbf{v}_i,
$$

 

where $\mathbf u_i$ and $\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  

The formula above works whenever $\sigma_i\neq 0.$ But how do we find the $i$th column of $U$ in cases where $\sigma_i = 0?$ It turns out that we can find the corresponding left singular vector using the geometric properties of singular values.

![](images/58/58af793e95fd96171530b2b63e74d12e965fb02eb81af42c8fdb3c9289a04b11.svg)

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 1 \\ 3 & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
